The user wants a long, detailed history of the Dutch water boards (waterschappen / hoogheemraadschappen), organized one era per paragraph. Let me think about what I know about this topic and structure it well.

The Dutch water boards are among the oldest forms of local government in the Netherlands, and indeed among the oldest functioning democratic institutions in the world. Let me organize the history into eras:

1. **Origins (c. 800–1250)**: Early medieval period. Before organized water management, people lived on natural high ground — river levees, dunes, boulder clay outcrops (like in Drenthe). Population growth, especially from around 800-1000 CE, pushed settlement onto lower peat lands. The Great Reclamation (Grote Ontginning) of the High Middle Ages (roughly 950-1350) saw organized colonization of peat bogs and marshlands, often led by lords who contracted colonists (copes/hoeven). Drainage of peat caused soil subsidence — peat dries, oxidizes, compacts. This meant land sank below water levels, requiring permanent drainage. Ditches were dug, water had to be drained to lower levels.
